title: Backcasting Probe Transfer: Does a Deception Probe Trained on One Scenario Catch Sabotage in Another?

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting Probe Transfer: Does a Deception Probe Trained on One Scenario Catch Sabotage in Another?

**Problem:** Success state: an activation monitor that generalizes — a probe trained on a few deception examples flags deception it never saw. Backward: we need to measure cross-scenario transfer of a simple linear probe on open weights, the bottleneck for real-time activation monitoring.

**Direction:** On an open model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B), fit a logistic linear probe on residual-stream activations for one deception scenario (e.g. insider-trading concealment prompts), then evaluate AUROC on a DIFFERENT scenario (e.g. sandbagging on a quiz). Report the transfer gap. Result: 'a probe-transfer matrix across deception types.'

**Why it matters:** Activation probes are a starred open problem, but their value hinges on out-of-distribution transfer. Linear probes on open weights are squarely within a beginner's reach on one GPU, and transfer-specific framing is fresh vs. the catalogued 'Activation Probe Generalization.'

**Relevant context:** 'Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes' (arXiv:2502.03407, AUROC 0.96-0.999 in-distribution, probe after layer 22 of Llama-3.3-70B); 'Pressure-Testing Deception Probes' (arXiv:2605.27958). Distinct from prior catalogue items by focusing on cross-scenario transfer matrix on a small 8B model.
